title: Composition versus inheritance
hook: A microservice host is a composition root: it owns collaborators, not a family tree. Inheritance is a scalpel for one is-a relationship with a virtual surface. C# forces the choice because you get only one base class.

sections.heading: What composition looks like in production
sections.prose: An SQS consumer that grades attempts does not inherit from RedisCache and RabbitPublisher. It receives IAttemptStore, IBus, and IClock through a constructor (module 04) and calls them. That is composition: has-a, replaceable in tests, versioned independently. Inheritance couples your type to a constructor chain and a protected surface you must keep forever. Across service boundaries, composition is how you stay deployable.

sections.heading: When inheritance still wins
sections.prose: Use a base class when many types share algorithm steps with variation points — a Template Method with protected abstract hooks — and you control all derived types in one assembly. A family of auth providers that only differ in how they parse a token can share validation and clock skew in a base, with sealed derived LtiProvider and OidcProvider. If the variation is a dependency (HTTP vs in-memory), inject it instead of subclassing.

snippets.label: Compose a worker; inherit only the parser family
snippets.explanation: The worker is sealed and composed. TokenParser is a narrow hierarchy for parsing variation. Redis and the bus stay interfaces, not base classes.

sections.heading: Interview phrasing
sections.prose: Say: “I inherit for polymorphism I own; I compose for infrastructure I replace.” Follow with C#’s single base class and interfaces for extra capabilities (next topics). Do not recite the GoF book; point at a worker you have shipped.

interviewTakeaways: Composition is has-a via constructor injection; inheritance is is-a with one base.
Microservices stay composition-heavy; hierarchies stay small and in-process.
Interfaces (later topic) are how C# adds extra roles without a second base class.
commonPitfalls: BaseService that becomes a dumping ground for logging, HTTP, and caching.
Subclassing to tweak one method when a delegate or strategy object would do.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS historically piled behavior on prototypes. Modern JS/TS services compose modules the same way C# workers compose interfaces.
TS mixins fake multiple inheritance. C# uses interfaces plus composition; there is no mixin keyword.
